books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: South Carolina, Declaration of the Immediate Causes of Secession (December 24, 1860)

stimulus.source_note: South Carolina, Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union, December 24, 1860. Public domain. Wording verified against the Bochum source collection (ruhr-uni-bochum.de/gna/Quellensammlung/05/05_southcarolinasecession_1860.htm) and the Hillsdale reprint. Passages appear in this order; '. . .' marks omitted text.
stimulus.text: . . . In the present case, that fact is established with certainty. We assert that fourteen of the States have deliberately refused for years past to fulfil their constitutional obligations, and we refer to their own Statutes for the proof. . . . Thus the constitutional compact has been deliberately broken and disregarded by the non-slaveholding States, and the consequence follows that South Carolina is released from her obligation. . . . A geographical line has been drawn across the Union, and all the States north of that line have united in the election of a man to the high office of President of the United States whose opinions and purposes are hostile to Slavery. . . . On the 4th of March next this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that the South shall be excluded from the common territory, that the judicial tribunals shall be made sectional, and that a war must be waged against Slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The declaration's claim that “a war must be waged against Slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States” best shows that South Carolina's leaders believed Lincoln's election meant

options.text: slavery itself, not just its expansion, was now threatened.
the South would be allowed to keep slavery forever.
options.misconception: The passage warns of war against slavery until it ends, the opposite of a guarantee.

options.text: the North would repeal the Fugitive Slave Act at once.
options.misconception: The passage charges the Northern states with refusing to enforce the fugitive-slave clause, not with repealing the act.

options.text: the Supreme Court would soon overturn Dred Scott.
options.misconception: The passage never mentions the Court or Dred Scott; its fear is the new president, not the judges.

rationales.A: South Carolina reads Lincoln's election as the start of a war on slavery everywhere, not only in the territories. Background: Lincoln had promised only to stop slavery's spread, but the declaration treats that as the first step toward ending it entirely.
rationales.B: The passage warns of war against slavery until it ends, the opposite of a guarantee.
rationales.C: The passage charges the Northern states with refusing to enforce the fugitive-slave clause, not with repealing the act.
rationales.D: The passage never mentions the Court or Dred Scott; its fear is the new president, not the judges.
rationales.general:
1. The declaration moves from broken promises to a prediction: war on slavery until it ends.
2. That prediction goes further than anything Lincoln had promised.
3. Background: Southern leaders argued that slavery had to grow to survive, so stopping its spread was a slow death sentence.
4. Fear of the future, not only anger at the past, drove secession.
Remember: secessionists argued from what they feared would happen next, not only from what had already happened.
